claim: Wnt/β-catenin signaling is essential for BBB development and maintenance in endothelial cells (ECs) in most CNS vessels.
source: Wnt/β-catenin signaling is essential for BBB development and maintenance in endothelial cells (ECs) in most CNS vessels.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work (Daneman et al., 2009; Stenman et al., 2008; Liebner et al., 2008; Zhou et al., 2014) as indicated in the abstract and introduction.

claim: CVO ECs rendered Wnt-reporter negative in mouse development, suggesting low level pathway activity.
source: Here we show that in mouse development, as well as in adult mouse and zebrafish, CVO ECs rendered Wnt-reporter negative, suggesting low level pathway activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from BAT-gal reporter mice and zebrafish reporter lines as described in the abstract and results sections.

claim: The subfornical organ (SFO) vasculature revealed heterogenous claudin-5 (Cldn5) and Plvap/Meca32 expression indicative for tight and leaky vessels, respectively.
source: Characterization of the subfornical organ (SFO) vasculature revealed heterogenous claudin-5 (Cldn5) and Plvap/Meca32 expression indicative for tight and leaky vessels, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical staining data presented in Figure 3 and related text.

claim: Dominant, EC-specific β-catenin transcription in mice converted phenotypically leaky into BBB-like vessels by augmenting Cldn5+ vessels.
source: Dominant, EC-specific β-catenin transcription in mice, converted phenotypically leaky into BBB-like vessels, by augmenting Cldn5+vessels, stabilizing junctions and by reducing Plvap/Meca32+ and fenestrated vessels, resulting in decreased tracer permeability.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from β-catenin GOF mice shown in Figures 4-7.

claim: Dominant, EC-specific β-catenin transcription in mice stabilized junctions.
source: Dominant, EC-specific β-catenin transcription in mice, converted phenotypically leaky into BBB-like vessels, by augmenting Cldn5+vessels, stabilizing junctions and by reducing Plvap/Meca32+ and fenestrated vessels, resulting in decreased tracer permeability.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data showing more elaborate junctional areas in GOF mice (Figure 7).

claim: Dominant, EC-specific β-catenin transcription in mice reduced Plvap/Meca32+ vessels.
source: Dominant, EC-specific β-catenin transcription in mice, converted phenotypically leaky into BBB-like vessels, by augmenting Cldn5+vessels, stabilizing junctions and by reducing Plvap/Meca32+ and fenestrated vessels, resulting in decreased tracer permeability.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Dominant, EC-specific β-catenin transcription in mice reduced fenestrated vessels.
source: Dominant, EC-specific β-catenin transcription in mice, converted phenotypically leaky into BBB-like vessels, by augmenting Cldn5+vessels, stabilizing junctions and by reducing Plvap/Meca32+ and fenestrated vessels, resulting in decreased tracer permeability.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy quantification showing significantly reduced fenestrations in GOF mice (Figure 7D).

claim: Dominant, EC-specific β-catenin transcription in mice resulted in decreased tracer permeability.
source: Dominant, EC-specific β-catenin transcription in mice, converted phenotypically leaky into BBB-like vessels, by augmenting Cldn5+vessels, stabilizing junctions and by reducing Plvap/Meca32+ and fenestrated vessels, resulting in decreased tracer permeability.
evidence: This is supported by FITC-albumin tracer experiments showing reduced leakage in GOF mice (Figure 6).

claim: Endothelial tightening augmented neuronal activity in the SFO of water restricted mice.
source: Endothelial tightening augmented neuronal activity in the SFO of water restricted mice.
evidence: This is supported by c-fos staining data showing increased neuronal activation in GOF mice under water restriction (Figure 9).

claim: Regulating the SFO vessel barrier may influence neuronal function in the context of water homeostasis.
source: Hence, regulating the SFO vessel barrier may influence neuronal function in the context of water homeostasis.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the observed increase in neuronal c-fos activity in GOF mice under water restriction.

claim: During developmental brain vascularization, blood vessels undergo Wnt/β-catenin signaling, driven by Wnt7a/7b that is required for angiogenesis as well as for BBB formation.
source: During developmental brain vascularization, blood vessels undergo Wnt/β-catenin signaling, driven by Wnt7a/7b that is required for angiogenesis as well as for BBB formation (Daneman et al., 2009; Stenman et al., 2008; Liebner et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In the adult, the Wnt pathway remains instrumental to maintain BBB function in endothelial cells (ECs) of the central nervous system (CNS).
source: In the adult, the Wnt pathway remains instrumental to maintain BBB function in endothelial cells (ECs) of the central nervous system (CNS) (Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Activation of β-catenin/TCF signaling can be induced by two flavors of the canonical Wnt pathway mediated by the ligands Wnt7a/7b and the non-Wnt-related norrin disease protein (Ndp).
source: Herein activation of β-catenin/TCF signaling can be induced by two flavors of the canonical Wnt pathway mediated by the ligands Wnt7a/7b and the non-Wnt-related norrin disease protein (Ndp), binding to the receptor complexes frizzled-4/Lrp5/6/Gpr124/Reck and frizzled-4/Lrp5/6/Tspan12, respectively (Junge et al., 2009; Chang et al., 2017; Cullen et al., 2011; Posokhova et al., 2015; Kuhnert et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2014; Cho et al., 2017; Vanhollebeke et al., 2015; Eubelen et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The circumventricular organs (CVOs) are a number of small midline structures found in all vertebrate brains, located around the third and fourth ventricle.
source: The circumventricular organs (CVOs) are a number of small midline structures found in all vertebrate brains, located around the third and fourth ventricle.
evidence: This is a statement of established anatomical knowledge.

claim: CVOs have a rich capillary plexus, which physiologically lacks BBB properties.
source: CVOs have a rich capillary plexus, which physiologically lacks BBB properties (Ganong, 2000; Ufnal and Skrzypecki, 2014; Langlet et al., 2013; Benarroch, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: CVOs are regarded as important sites of communication between brain and blood.
source: These characteristics are regarded as important sites of communication between brain and blood.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical and physiological properties of CVOs described in the literature.

claim: Based on their function, CVOs are commonly classified into secretory and sensory organs.
source: Based on their function, CVOs are commonly classified into secretory and sensory organs.
evidence: This is a statement of established classification in the field.

claim: The median eminence, the neurohypophysis (posterior pituitary, PP), the pineal gland (PI) and the subcommissural organ (SCO) belong to the secretory group.
source: The median eminence, the neurohypophysis (posterior pituitary, PP), the pineal gland (PI) and the subcommissural organ (SCO) belong to the secretory group.
evidence: This is a statement of established classification in the field.

claim: The vascular organ of the lamina terminalis (organum vasculosum of the lamina terminalis, OVLT), the subfornical organ (SFO) and the area postrema (AP) are considered as sensory organs.
source: The vascular organ of the lamina terminalis (organum vasculosum of the lamina terminalis, OVLT), the subfornical organ (SFO) and the area postrema (AP) are considered as sensory organs (Ufnal and Skrzypecki, 2014).
evidence: This is a statement of established classification in the field, supported by a citation.

claim: The leaky vessels of the CVOs evidently have different morphological and structural characteristics from those of typical BBB vessels, lacking a cellular organization as neuro-vascular unit (NVU), without distinctive astrocytic endfeet and ECs with numerous fenestrations and vesicles.
source: The leaky vessels of the CVOs evidently have different morphological and structural characteristics from those of typical BBB vessels, lacking a cellular organization as neuro-vascular unit (NVU), without distinctive astrocytic endfeet and ECs with numerous fenestrations and vesicles (Morita et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Neither the tight junction proteins claudin-5 (Cldn5), occludin (Ocln) and zonula occludens 1 (Tjp1/ZO-1), nor the transporter proteins glucose transporter 1 (Glut-1) and transferrin receptor, showed a BBB-like staining in leaky CVO ECs.
source: Interestingly, in previous reports neither the tight junction proteins claudin-5 (Cldn5), occludin (Ocln) and zonula occludens 1 (Tjp1/ZO-1) (Mullier et al., 2010; Maolood and Meister, 2010; Norsted et al., 2008; Sisó et al., 2010), nor the transporter proteins glucose transporter 1 (Glut-1) and transferrin receptor (Norsted et al., 2008; Maolood and Meister, 2009), showed a BBB-like staining in leaky CVO ECs.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Morita et al. showed that 10 kDa dextran accumulates in the perivascular space between the inner and outer basement membranes, whereas smaller tracers up to 3 kDa dextran diffuse into the parenchyma.
source: In line with these vascular features, Morita et al. showed that 10 kDa dextran accumulates in the perivascular space between the inner and outer basement membranes, whereas smaller tracers up to 3 kDa dextran diffuse into the parenchyma (Morita et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The perivascular space in CVOs is enlarged and filled by collagen fibers, fibroblasts, astrocytic processes and axons.
source: Not only the endothelium, but also the perivascular space in CVOs has specific properties, being enlarged and filled by collagen fibers, fibroblasts, astrocytic processes and axons (Morita and Miyata, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Free diffusion of substances into the brain parenchyma is prohibited by tanycytes, specialized cells of the ependymal lining.
source: Beside the leaky vasculature of the CVOs, free diffusion of substances into the brain parenchyma is prohibited by tanycytes, specialized cells of the ependymal lining.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about tanycyte function.

claim: Tanycytes contain long processes, unlike typical ependymal cells, which project to the parenchyma of the CVOs making contact to the fenestrated vascular wall of the CVOs.
source: Tanycytes contain long processes, unlike typical ependymal cells, which project to the parenchyma of the CVOs making contact to the fenestrated vascular wall of the CVOs (Langlet et al., 2013; Benarroch, 2011; Mullier et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The SFO together with the OVLT, the median preoptic nucleus (MnPO) and the PP were identified as a functional circuit, regulating drinking behavior and water homeostasis of the organism.
source: The detailed function of all CVOs has not intensely been explored in the past, but more recently, the SFO together with the OVLT, the median preoptic nucleus (MnPO) and the PP were identified as a functional circuit, regulating drinking behavior and water homeostasis of the organism (Zimmerman et al., 2016; Oka et al., 2015; Augustine et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The SFO is a tiny organ located underneath the fornix at the foramen of Monro, protruding into the third ventricle at the meeting point with the lateral ventricles.
source: The SFO is a tiny organ located underneath the fornix at the foramen of Monro, protruding into the third ventricle at the meeting point with the lateral ventricles.
evidence: This is a statement of established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The dense vascular network in the SFO is similarly organized in different vertebrate species.
source: The dense vascular network in the SFO is similarly organized in different vertebrate species.
evidence: This is a statement of established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The SFO presents with heterogeneous vessel phenotypes and can therefore be divided into two zones.
source: It presents with heterogeneous vessel phenotypes and can therefore be divided into two zones.
evidence: This is a statement of established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The outer shell of the SFO contains more BBB expressing vessels, whereas the majority within the ventromedial core is fenestrated with a wide perivascular space.
source: Whereas the outer shell contains more BBB expressing vessels, the majority within the ventromedial core is fenestrated with a wide perivascular space.
evidence: This is a statement of established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The vascular density in the SFO is four to five times higher than in other brain regions with tortuous vessels, exhibiting a high blood volume and slow perfusion rate, thereby contributing to high permeability rates.
source: In general, the vascular density is four to five times higher than in other brain regions with tortuous vessels, exhibiting a high blood volume and slow perfusion rate, thereby contributing to high permeability rates (Sisó et al., 2010; Duvernoy and Risold, 2007; Fry et al., 2007; Bouchaud et al., 1989).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Neurons and astrocytes of sensory CVOs (SFO, OVLT and AP) express specific receptors and ion channels.
source: Although a cell type-specific expression analysis by single cell sequencing, as it has been performed for the brain parenchyma (Vanlandewijck et al., 2018), has not been conducted yet, neurons and astrocytes of sensory CVOs (SFO, OVLT and AP) were shown to express specific receptors and ion channels.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Specific receptors and ion channels in sensory CVOs permit neurons and astrocytes to detect several blood–derived molecules such as salts, hormones, lipids and toxins and convey this information to other parts of the brain, involved in controlling autonomic and peripheral functions.
source: Those permit them to detect several blood–derived molecules such as salts, hormones, lipids and toxins and convey this information to other parts of the brain, involved in controlling autonomic and peripheral functions (Benarroch, 2011; Sisó et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Evidence supports that 25–60% of CVO neurons respond to signals in the circulatory system and a single neuron may respond to multiple signals such as osmolarity and angiotensin II.
source: Evidence supports that 25–60% of CVO neurons respond to signals in the circulatory system and a single neuron may respond to multiple signals such as osmolarity and angiotensin II.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Most sensory CVOs play a role in the control of blood pressure, fluid and sodium balance, cardiovascular regulation, feeding and energy homeostasis and immunomodulation.
source: Most sensory CVOs play a role in the control of blood pressure, fluid and sodium balance, cardiovascular regulation, feeding and energy homeostasis and immunomodulation (Ufnal and Skrzypecki, 2014; Benarroch, 2011; Sisó et al., 2010; Morita and Miyata, 2012; Smith and Ferguson, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: At any embryonic stage analyzed, starting from E13.5, when the first SFO primordium could be identified, to P21, no activation of β-catenin signaling in CVO vessels could be detected in BAT-gal reporter mice.
source: Here we show by investigating CVOs during BAT-gal reporter mouse development that at any embryonic stage analyzed, starting from E13.5, when the first SFO primordium could be identified, to P21, no activation of β-catenin signaling in CVO vessels could be detected.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from BAT-gal reporter mice shown in Figure 1 and supplements.

claim: Blood vessels in the caudal portion of the SFO were mainly leaky evidenced by Plvap/Meca32 staining.
source: Focusing on the SFO as a crucial CVO in the regulation of water homeostasis, we show that blood vessels in the caudal portion were mainly leaky evidenced by Plvap/Meca32 staining, whereas capillaries in the rostral portion of the organ were tighter.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Capillaries in the rostral portion of the SFO were tighter.
source: Focusing on the SFO as a crucial CVO in the regulation of water homeostasis, we show that blood vessels in the caudal portion were mainly leaky evidenced by Plvap/Meca32 staining, whereas capillaries in the rostral portion of the organ were tighter.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Within the vessel continuity, individual ECs might be Plvap/Meca32+//Cldn5- followed by a Plvap/Meca32-//Cldn5+ EC, suggesting a locally confined regulation of barrier properties.
source: Interestingly, within the vessel continuity, individual ECs might be Plvap/Meca32+//Cldn5- followed by a Plvap/Meca32-//Cldn5+ EC, suggesting a locally confined regulation of barrier properties.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Dominant, genetic activation of β-catenin signaling (gain-of-function, GOF) in ECs resulted in tightening of CVO blood vessels, evidenced by the switch from a Plvap/Meca32+//Cldn5- to a Plvap/Meca32-//Cldn5+ vascular phenotype.
source: Dominant, genetic activation of β-catenin signaling (gain-of-function, GOF) in ECs resulted in tightening of CVO blood vessels, evidenced by the switch from a Plvap/Meca32+//Cldn5- to a Plvap/Meca32-//Cldn5+ vascular phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Vessel tightening was accompanied by a significant reduction in endothelial fenestrations.
source: Vessel tightening was accompanied by a significant reduction in endothelial fenestrations, that likely contributed to the reduction of transcellular permeability evidenced by decreased tracer leakage.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Reduction in endothelial fenestrations likely contributed to the reduction of transcellular permeability evidenced by decreased tracer leakage.
source: Vessel tightening was accompanied by a significant reduction in endothelial fenestrations, that likely contributed to the reduction of transcellular permeability evidenced by decreased tracer leakage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed reduction in fenestrations and tracer leakage data shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Endothelial tightening did not coincide with the formation of astrocytic endfeet towards a BBB-like NVU.
source: Interestingly, endothelial tightening did not coincide with the formation of astrocytic endfeet towards a BBB-like NVU.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data for astrocytic markers shown in Figure 7 supplements.

claim: We observed augmented neuronal activity in the SFO under thirst conditions after sealing CVO vessels, supported by significantly increased neuronal c-fos staining in the SFO of GOF mice.
source: Finally, we observed augmented neuronal activity in the SFO under thirst conditions after sealing CVO vessels, supported by significantly increased neuronal c-fos staining in the SFO of GOF mice.
evidence: This is supported by c-fos staining data shown in Figure 9.

claim: BAT-gal mice report active Wnt/β-catenin in brain parenchymal vessels during embryonic and early postnatal brain vascularization.
source: As previously shown, BAT-gal mice report active Wnt/β-catenin in brain parenchymal vessels during embryonic and early postnatal brain vascularization (Figure 1A) (Liebner et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and a citation to prior work.

claim: E13.5 was the first timepoint we could identify the primordial SFO.
source: We made use of BAT-gal mice to monitor Wnt/β-catenin activity in CVO vessels at different time points of embryonic and postnatal mouse development, starting from E13.5 which was the first timepoint we could identify the primordial SFO, to P21 (Figure 1B–E, Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a statement based on the authors' experimental observations.

claim: In the SFO we could not detect an overlap of reporter gene-expression and CD31+ cells at any developmental stage analyzed.
source: In the SFO (Figure 1B–E) we could not detect an overlap of reporter gene-expression and CD31+ cells at any developmental stage analyzed.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 1B-E.

claim: Adjacent, non-endothelial cells in the ependymal lining as well as cells in the stroma of the SFO showed active Wnt/β-catenin signaling, evidenced by nuclear β-galactosidase staining.
source: Instead, adjacent, non-endothelial cells in the ependymal lining as well as cells in the stroma of the organ showed active Wnt/β-catenin signaling, evidenced by nuclear β-galactosidase staining (Figure 1B–E).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 1B-E.

claim: The observation that adjacent, non-endothelial cells in the SFO show Wnt/β-catenin signaling suggested that Wnt growth factors are indeed available in the CVO region, but the canonical pathway was not activated in ECs.
source: The latter observation suggested that Wnt growth factors are indeed available in the CVO region, but the canonical pathway was not activated in ECs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of Wnt pathway activity in non-endothelial cells but not in ECs.

claim: We did not observe reporter gene-expressing ECs in the OVLT and in the PI.
source: Similarly, we did also not observe reporter gene-expressing ECs in the OVLT and in the PI (Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2), providing evidence for the interpretation that CVO endothelia generally show low or no Wnt/β-catenin activity.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 1 supplements 1 and 2.

claim: CVO endothelia generally show low or no Wnt/β-catenin activity.
source: Similarly, we did also not observe reporter gene-expressing ECs in the OVLT and in the PI (Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2), providing evidence for the interpretation that CVO endothelia generally show low or no Wnt/β-catenin activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of reporter gene expression in multiple CVOs.

claim: In all zebrafish analyzed, OVLT vessels were largely devoid of GFP reporter gene expression.
source: In all fish analyzed, OVLT vessels were largely devoid of GFP reporter gene expression, suggesting that Wnt/β-catenin activation is strongly reduced or absent in this CVO of the fish (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin activation is strongly reduced or absent in the OVLT of zebrafish.
source: In all fish analyzed, OVLT vessels were largely devoid of GFP reporter gene expression, suggesting that Wnt/β-catenin activation is strongly reduced or absent in this CVO of the fish (Figure 2).
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of reporter gene expression in zebrafish OVLT vessels.

claim: The lack of Wnt pathway activation in CVO vessels is evolutionary conserved.
source: We further wanted to address the question, whether the lack of Wnt pathway activation in CVO vessels is evolutionary conserved and analyzed the OVLT of adult Wnt pathway reporter zebrafish (Jeong et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of low Wnt pathway activity in both mouse and zebrafish CVOs.

claim: Vessels in the SFO, OVLT and PP were Plvap/Meca32+, but also showed a considerable degree of intermingling with Cldn5+ ECs.
source: In order to visualize the organs, relevant for water homeostasis, we initially applied fluorescent microscopy on sagittal sections, showing that indeed, vessels in the SFO, OVLT and PP were Plvap/Meca32+, but also showed a considerable degree of intermingling with Cldn5+ ECs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 3 supplement 1.

claim: Light sheet microscopy analysis of whole mount preparations revealed that the majority of SFO vessels in the rostral portion, as well as of the shell were Plvap/Meca32-//Cldn5+, suggesting that these vessels possess BBB properties.
source: Light sheet microscopy analysis of whole mount preparations revealed that the majority of SFO vessels in the rostral portion, as well as of the shell were Plvap/Meca32-//Cldn5+, suggesting that these vessels possess BBB properties.
evidence: This is supported by light sheet microscopy data shown in Figure 3D and Video 1.

claim: Vessels of the caudal SFO region were mainly Plvap/Meca32+//Cldn5-, providing evidence for their leaky phenotype.
source: Instead, vessels of the caudal SFO region were mainly Plvap/Meca32+//Cldn5-, providing evidence for their leaky phenotype (Figure 3D; Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by light sheet microscopy data shown in Figure 3D and Video 1.

claim: Higher magnification of the rostral part and the outer shell of the SFO showed that some vessels exhibit a mosaic-like staining for Plvap/Meca32 and Cldn5 along their longitudinal extension.
source: Higher magnification of the rostral part and the outer shell of the organ showed that some vessels exhibit a mosaic-like staining for Plvap/Meca32 and Cldn5 along their longitudinal extension (Figure 3D; Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by light sheet microscopy data shown in Figure 3D and Video 1.

claim: Confocal microscopy on sagittal sections revealed that neighboring cells may be positive either for Plvap/Meca32 or for Cldn5.
source: In order to visualize the alternating expression of leaky and tight vessel markers in more detail, we applied confocal microscopy on sagittal sections, revealing that neighboring cells may be positive either for Plvap/Meca32 or for Cldn5 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Some cells showed a mixed identity, allowing the interpretation that there is a continuous transition from leaky-to-tight-to-leaky vessels in the SFO.
source: However, some cells also showed a mixed identity, allowing the interpretation that there is a continuous transition from leaky-to-tight-to-leaky vessels in the SFO.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of cells with mixed marker expression.

claim: Cdh5(PAC)-CreERT2:Ctnnb1E×3fl/fl (GOF) double-transgenic mice were induced with tamoxifen (TAM) either directly after birth for three (50 µg/day, P1-P3) or in the adult for five (500 µg/day, 8–10 week-old mice) consecutive days.
source: To dominantly activate the Wnt/β-catenin pathway in ECs, Cdh5(PAC)-CreERT2:Ctnnb1E×3fl/fl (GOF) double-transgenic mice were induced with tamoxifen (TAM) either directly after birth for three (50 µg/day, P1-P3, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) or in the adult for five (500 µg/day, 8–10 week-old mice, Figure 4) consecutive days.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: At both timepoints analyzed (P6 and P14), control vessels exhibited high levels of Plvap/Meca32 and low levels of Cldn5 immunolabeling.
source: At both timepoints analyzed (P6 and P14), control vessels exhibited high levels of Plvap/Meca32 and low levels of Cldn5 immunolabeling (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 4 supplement 1A,B.

claim: Endothelial-specific β-catenin GOF reverted the leaky phenotype, resulting in significantly decreased Plvap/Meca32 immunoreactivity, whereas Cldn5 expression was markedly increased in these vessels without any changes in VE-cadherin immunolabeling at P6.
source: Interestingly, endothelial-specific β-catenin GOF reverted this phenotype, resulting in significantly decreased Plvap/Meca32 immunoreactivity, whereas Cldn5 expression was markedly increased in these vessels without any changes in VE-cadherin immunolabeling at P6 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data and quantification shown in Figure 4 supplement 1C.

claim: In the adult, the same antagonistic regulation of Plvap/Meca32 and Cldn5 by β-catenin GOF was observed as in postnatal stages.
source: In the adult, the same antagonistic regulation of Plvap/Meca32 and Cldn5 by β-catenin GOF was observed as in postnatal stages (Figure 4B–D; quantification 4E, F).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 4B-F.

claim: Activation of β-catenin signaling significantly suppressed Plvap/Meca32 and induced Cldn5 already by day 16.
source: When analyzing different timepoints after TAM induction of adult GOF mice for the expression of Plvap/Meca32 and Cldn5, we observed that activation of β-catenin signaling significantly suppressed Plvap/Meca32 and induced Cldn5 already by day 16 (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data and quantification shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: Maximal Cldn5 induction was observed after 26 days, being significantly higher than at day 19 after the first TAM injection.
source: Maximal Cldn5 induction was observed after 26 days, being significantly higher than at day 19 after the first TAM injection (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data and quantification shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Analysis of pooled mRNA from 17 whole SFOs from GOF or control mice revealed that Plvap/Meca32 was indeed down-regulated in the GOF condition on the mRNA level.
source: Analysis of pooled mRNA from 17 whole SFOs from GOF or control mice, revealed that Plvap/Meca32 was indeed down-regulated in the GOF condition on the mRNA level, whereas Cldn5 did not show an obvious regulation.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Cldn5 did not show an obvious regulation on the mRNA level in GOF condition.
source: Analysis of pooled mRNA from 17 whole SFOs from GOF or control mice, revealed that Plvap/Meca32 was indeed down-regulated in the GOF condition on the mRNA level, whereas Cldn5 did not show an obvious regulation.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Transformation of the leaky into a tight vessel phenotype in the SFO by β-catenin GOF requires around 26 days after induction of recombination.
source: This suggested that transformation of the leaky into a tight vessel phenotype in the SFO by β-catenin GOF requires around 26 days after induction of recombination.
evidence: This is an inference based on the time course data showing maximal Cldn5 induction at 26 days.

claim: Analyzing the junctional localization of Ocln normalized to the vessel length in the SFO, we observed only a punctuated staining of Ocln at endothelial cell-cell junctions of controls as previously described by Morita et al.
source: Analyzing the junctional localization of Ocln normalized to the vessel length in the SFO, we observed only a punctuated staining of Ocln at endothelial cell-cell junctions of controls as previously described by Morita et al. (Morita and Miyata, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 5 and a citation to prior work.

claim: In vessels of GOF mice we noted a significant increase in line-like junctional Ocln staining compared to controls.
source: In vessels of GOF mice we noted a significant increase in line-like junctional Ocln staining compared to controls (Figure 5A,B; quantification Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data and quantification shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Analysis of mRNA of pooled SFO samples from GOF or control mice revealed that Ocln, like Cldn5, did not show an obvious regulation in the GOF condition.
source: Further analysis of mRNA of pooled SFO samples from GOF or control mice, revealed that Ocln, like Cldn5, did not show an obvious regulation in the GOF condition (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: ZO-1 showed only a moderately increased localization at cell-cell junctions in SFO vessels of GOF mice.
source: As opposed to Cldn5 and Ocln, ZO-1 showed only a moderately increased localization at cell-cell junctions in SFO vessels of GOF mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 5 supplement 1.

claim: ZO-1 was consistently present at inter-endothelial junctions of the SFO in the control condition.
source: Specifically, ZO-1 was consistently present at inter-endothelial junctions of the SFO in the control condition.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 5 supplement 1.

claim: Analysis of FITC-BSA leakage normalized to vessel area revealed a significant reduction of extravasation in SFO vessels of the GOF versus control mice.
source: Analysis of FITC-BSA leakage normalized to vessel area revealed a significant reduction of extravasation in SFO vessels of the GOF versus control mice (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by tracer leakage data and quantification shown in Figure 6.

claim: The leaky vessels in the controls showed pronounced FITC-BSA distribution in the circumference of vessels indicated by a prominent cloudy FITC signal in the entire SFO, whereas in the GOF condition the tracer remained confined to the vessel lumen.
source: Specifically, the leaky vessels in the controls showed pronounced FITC-BSA distribution in the circumference of vessels indicated by a prominent cloudy FITC signal in the entire SFO, whereas in the GOF condition the tracer remained confined to the vessel lumen (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by tracer leakage data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: β-catenin GOF experiments with the Pdgfb-iCreERT2 mouse driver line resulted in comparable regulation of Plvap/Meca32 and Cldn5.
source: To strengthen the observation of SFO vessel tightening, we performed β-catenin GOF experiments also with the Pdgfb-iCreERT2 mouse driver line (Claxton et al., 2008), resulting in comparable regulation of Plvap/Meca32 and Cldn5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 4 supplement 3A,B.

claim: Activation of the Wnt/β-catenin pathway was supported by significantly increased nuclear Sox17 localization.
source: Activation of the Wnt/β-catenin pathway was supported by significantly increased nuclear Sox17 localization that was reported to be a downstream target of Wnt/β-catenin and to be upstream of Notch (Corada et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2015) (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C,D).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data and quantification shown in Figure 4 supplement 3C,D, and citations to prior work.

claim: Sox17 was reported to be a downstream target of Wnt/β-catenin and to be upstream of Notch.
source: Activation of the Wnt/β-catenin pathway was supported by significantly increased nuclear Sox17 localization that was reported to be a downstream target of Wnt/β-catenin and to be upstream of Notch (Corada et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2015) (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C,D).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Leaky SFO vessels did not exhibit pronounced staining of the polarity markers αDag and Kir4.1.
source: As previously shown for astrocytic endfeet proteins (Pócsai and Kálmán, 2015), leaky SFO vessels did not exhibit pronounced staining of the polarity markers αDag and Kir4.1 (Figure 7—figure supplements 1B,C and and 2B,C).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 7 supplements 1 and 2, and a citation to prior work.

claim: None of the astrocytic endfeet markers were found to be affected by the GOF conditions.
source: Moreover, none of these stainings were found to be affected by the GOF conditions, meaning that no distinct staining of vascular endfeet could be observed.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 7 supplements 1 and 2.

claim: Aqp4 and αDag showed only a weak, unpolarized localization around vessels in GOF and controls.
source: Specifically, Aqp4 and αDag showed only a weak, unpolarized localization around vessels in GOF and controls, whereas the sodium channel Kir4.1 was mainly expressed by cells morphologically resembling tanycytes in the SFO (Figure 7—figure supplements 1B,C and and 2B,C).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 7 supplements 1 and 2.

claim: The sodium channel Kir4.1 was mainly expressed by cells morphologically resembling tanycytes in the SFO.
source: Specifically, Aqp4 and αDag showed only a weak, unpolarized localization around vessels in GOF and controls, whereas the sodium channel Kir4.1 was mainly expressed by cells morphologically resembling tanycytes in the SFO (Figure 7—figure supplements 1B,C and and 2B,C).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 7 supplements 1 and 2.

claim: The ECM components Lama2 and ColIV revealed that in GOF and in control vessels of the SFO a vascular and an astrocytic basal lamina was present with no obvious differences in structure and distribution between conditions.
source: The ECM components Lama2 and ColIV, revealed that in GOF and in control vessels of the SFO a vascular and an astrocytic basal lamina was present with no obvious differences in structure and distribution between conditions (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 7 supplement 2.

claim: The vessels in control SFOs showed the typical large and lacuna-like structure with an extensive ECM circumference.
source: As expected, the vessels in control SFOs showed the typical large and lacuna-like structure with an extensive ECM circumference (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7A-C.

claim: Fenestrations were frequently observed in the control condition, a morphological feature that is consistent with a high Plvap/Meca32 expression and a permeable phenotype.
source: Moreover, fenestrations were frequently observed in the control condition, a morphological feature that is consistent with a high Plvap/Meca32 expression and a permeable phenotype (Figure 7C; quantification Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data and quantification shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: The vessels of the GOF mice appeared to have a more compact ECM deposition in their circumference.
source: Although the vessel morphology did not show major differences regarding vessel perimeter and structure, the vessels of the GOF mice appeared to have a more compact ECM deposition in their circumference (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7A-C.

claim: Endothelial vesicles did not show obvious alterations between GOF and controls.
source: Endothelial vesicles did not show obvious alterations between GOF and controls (data not shown).
evidence: This is a statement based on the authors' observations, though the data are not shown.

claim: The junctional area of GOF vessels was considerably more elaborate compared to the controls, which exhibited typical blunt-ending connections.
source: Instead, the junctional area of GOF vessels was considerably more elaborate compared to the controls, which exhibited typical blunt-ending connections (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Fenestrations were significantly reduced in GOF mice, being in line with the reduction of Plvap/Meca32 immunostaining and further suggesting that β-catenin GOF in ECs is crucial for the suppression of a leaky vessel phenotype.
source: Additionally, fenestrations were significantly reduced in GOF mice, being in line with the reduction of Plvap/Meca32 immunostaining (Figure 4E; quantification Figure 4G) and further suggesting that β-catenin GOF in ECs is crucial for the suppression of a leaky vessel phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy quantification shown in Figure 7D and immunohistochemical data in Figure 4.

claim: Both thirst-inducing paradigms lead to a significant increase in c-fos+ neurons in the SFO of WT mice.
source: Both thirst-inducing paradigms lead to a significant increase in c-fos+ neurons in the SFO of WT mice (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by c-fos staining data and quantification shown in Figure 8.

claim: We could show a dose-dependent c-fos activation in thirst induction by hyperosmolar NaCl, comparing 2 M and 3 M solutions.
source: We could also show a dose-dependent c-fos activation in thirst induction by hyperosmolar NaCl, comparing 2 M and 3 M solutions (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by c-fos staining data and quantification shown in Figure 8 supplement 1.

claim: Under control conditions, in which mice received water ad libitum, we could not detect any genotype-specific differences in c-fos+ nuclei in the SFO between control and GOF animals.
source: Under control conditions, in which mice received water ad libitum, we could not detect any genotype-specific differences in c-fos+ nuclei in the SFO between control and GOF animals (data not shown).
evidence: This is a statement based on the authors' observations, though the data are not shown.

claim: Water restriction for 72 hrs induced a slight, but stable weight loss in GOF and control mice in the same manner.
source: In case of water restriction for 72 hrs (Figure 9A) a slight, but stable weight loss was induced in GOF and control mice in the same manner (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is supported by body weight monitoring data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Analysis of c-fos activation revealed a significantly higher neuronal activity in the SFO of GOF mice under water restriction.
source: Analysis of c-fos activation revealed a significantly higher neuronal activity in the SFO of GOF mice (Figure 9D).
evidence: This is supported by c-fos staining data and quantification shown in Figure 9C,D.

claim: Tightening SFO blood vessels may have physiological consequences for the water homeostasis in mice.
source: This suggests that tightening SFO blood vessels may have physiological consequences for the water homeostasis in mice.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the observed increase in neuronal c-fos activity in GOF mice under water restriction.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin signaling is undetectable in CVO vessels during BAT-gal reporter mouse development.
source: The principle findings of this study are: 1) Wnt/β-catenin signaling is undetectable in CVO vessels during BAT-gal reporter mouse development;
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings supported by data in Figure 1 and supplements.

claim: β-catenin-mediated transcription is strongly reduced in the adult zebrafish OVLT.
source: 2) similarly, β-catenin-mediated transcription is strongly reduced in the adult zebrafish OVLT;
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: SFO vessels are heterogenous regarding the expression of Plvap/Meca32 and Cldn5.
source: 3) SFO vessels are heterogenous regarding the expression of Plvap/Meca32 and Cldn5;
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Upon genetic β-catenin GOF in ECs, leaky SFO vessels are partially converted into tight vessels.
source: 4) upon genetic β-catenin GOF in ECs, leaky SFO vessels are partially converted into tight vessels;
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings supported by data in Figures 4-7.

claim: Functional conversion of SFO vessel towards a BBB-like identity affects neuronal activity in the SFO.
source: 5) functional conversion of SFO vessel towards a BBB-like identity affects neuronal activity in the SFO.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings supported by data in Figure 9.

claim: It has been shown that expression of the soluble frizzled receptor protein 1 (Sfrp1) is about 30 times higher in the rat choroid plexus (CP), that also lacks BBB vessels, compared to the striatum and parietal cortex.
source: So far, no conclusive data are available demonstrating Wnt pathway inhibitors in the CVOs, however, it has been shown that expression of the soluble frizzled receptor protein 1 (Sfrp1) is about 30 times higher in the rat choroid plexus (CP), that also lacks BBB vessels, compared to the striatum and parietal cortex (Bowyer et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: A detailed analysis of the CVOs regarding cell type-specific expression profiles has not been published yet.
source: Nevertheless, a detailed analysis of the CVOs regarding cell type-specific expression profiles has not been published yet.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Differentially tight vessels were also shown in other CVOs.
source: Similarly, differentially tight vessels were also shown in other CVOs (Morita and Miyata, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The present findings may suggest that, at least to some degree, vascular phenotypes in the SFO are locally regulated.
source: The present findings may suggest that, at least to some degree, vascular phenotypes in the SFO are locally regulated, which would be in line with their role providing local access for neurons to the blood milieu.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observed heterogeneity of vessel phenotypes.

claim: If vessel differentiation might also be dynamically regulated to control water homeostasis in a circadian rhythm is currently unknown and subject to ongoing investigation.
source: If vessel differentiation might also be dynamically regulated to control water homeostasis in a circadian rhythm (Gizowski et al., 2016), is currently unknown and subject to ongoing investigation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions.

claim: Cldn5 and Ocln might not be transcriptionally regulated by β-catenin, but rather regulated on a post-transcriptional level.
source: This might be due to several reasons, such as signal masking by other vessels in the whole mount preparations. Alternatively, this finding might support the interpretation that Cldn5 and Ocln are not transcriptionally regulated by β-catenin, but rather regulated on a post-transcriptional level.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the lack of mRNA regulation despite protein upregulation.

claim: There is still some controversy about Cldn5 regulation by Wnt/β-catenin.
source: Interestingly, there is still some controversy about Cldn5 regulation by Wnt/β-catenin, as it has been shown by Taddei et al. that β-catenin cooperates with FOXO1 to suppress Cldn5 at the promotor level under pro-angiogenic conditions (Taddei et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: It has been shown that Sox18, a member of the SOX family of high-mobility group box transcription factors, is instrumental in activating Cldn5 transcription, contributing to endothelial barrier formation.
source: On the other hand, it has been shown that Sox18, a member of the SOX family of high-mobility group box transcription factors, is instrumental in activating Cldn5 transcription, contributing to endothelial barrier formation (Fontijn et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Given the high redundancy of SoxF genes (Sox7, 17, 18), it might be feasible that Sox17, that we report here to be upregulated in SFO vessels of β-catenin GOF mice, mediates Cldn5 regulation.
source: Given the high redundancy of SoxF genes (Sox7, 17, 18) (Zhou et al., 2015), it might be feasible that Sox17, that we report here to be upregulated in SFO vessels of β-catenin GOF mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), mediates Cldn5 regulation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observed Sox17 upregulation and known SoxF gene redundancy.

claim: The tightening of SFO vessels by Cldn5 protein upregulation in β-catenin GOF mice is consistent with previous reports in other regions of the brain.
source: Although the regulation of Cldn5 on the promotor level and the role of β-catenin herein requires additional investigation, the tightening of SFO vessels by Cldn5 protein upregulation in β-catenin GOF mice is consistent with previous reports in other regions of the brain (Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The fact that ZO-1 exhibits also junctional staining in the controls is consistent with its role in VE-cadherin-based adherens junctions, which are also formed by SFO vessels.
source: The fact that ZO-1 exhibits also junctional staining in the controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), is consistent with its role in VE-cadherin-based adherens junctions, which are also formed by SFO vessels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) (Tornavaca et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 5 supplement 1 and Figure 4 supplement 1, and a citation to prior work.

claim: Endothelial β-catenin GOF resulted in the abolishment of fenestrations and strengthened inter-endothelial junctions, which are well in line with a reduction in VEGF signaling in glioma ECs upon Wnt/β-catenin activation via the downregulation of VEGF receptor 2 (VEGFR2, flk-1) and upregulation of VEGFR1.
source: Beside the mere upregulation of Cldn5 and Ocln, endothelial β-catenin GOF resulted in the abolishment of fenestrations and strengthened inter-endothelial junctions. These findings are well in line with a reduction in VEGF signaling in glioma ECs upon Wnt/β-catenin activation via the downregulation of VEGF receptor 2 (VEGFR2, flk-1) and upregulation of VEGFR1 (Reis et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by data in Figure 7 and a citation to prior work.

claim: Upon β-catenin GOF in CVO vessels the responsiveness of ECs for VEGF could be reduced, leading to regression of fenestrations.
source: This suggests that also upon β-catenin GOF in CVO vessels the responsiveness of ECs for VEGF could be reduced, leading to regression of fenestrations.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on prior work showing VEGF receptor regulation by Wnt/β-catenin.

claim: To form the NVU structure might require additional cues and/or prolonged time to form.
source: Hence, to form the NVU structure might require additional cues and/or prolonged time to form, although the latter explanation might not be as likely as the first, given that even after sixty days after TAM injection the control-like phenotype persisted (data not shown).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the lack of NVU formation in GOF mice.

claim: Tightening the ECs in the SFO via β-catenin GOF does not lead to pronounced structural alterations at the NVU.
source: These findings support the conclusion that tightening the ECs in the SFO via β-catenin GOF does not lead to pronounced structural alterations at the NVU.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the lack of changes in astrocytic endfeet and ECM markers.

claim: It might be therapeutically beneficial that the NVU is not affected by the dominant activation of endothelial β-catenin.
source: As the leaky vessels of the SFO core are surrounded by a prominent perivascular space, which is considered to be important for the communication of neuronal axons with the blood milieu, it might be therapeutically beneficial that the NVU is not affected by the dominant activation of endothelial β-catenin.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic implications.

claim: It was shown for the SFO that two distinct populations of neurons expressing ETV-1 and Vgat mediate thirst-ON and thirst-OFF signals, respectively.
source: Specifically, it was shown for the SFO that two distinct populations of neurons expressing ETV-1 and Vgat mediate thirst-ON and thirst-OFF signals, respectively (Oka et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: We provide evidence for an essential role of endothelial barrier function in neuronal activation in water restricted mice, as neuronal c-fos reactivity was increased in water-deprived GOF animals.
source: Here we provide evidence for an essential role of endothelial barrier function in neuronal activation in water restricted mice, as neuronal c-fos reactivity was increased in water-deprived GOF animals (Figure 9).
evidence: This is supported by c-fos staining data shown in Figure 9.

claim: How the finding of increased c-fos in GOF mice relates to the drinking behavior and to the activity of excitatory and inhibitory neuronal signals to and from the median preoptic nucleus (MnPO), which was shown to host the behavioral output neurons, is beyond the scope of this study and is subject to future work.
source: How this finding relates to the drinking behavior and to the activity of excitatory and inhibitory neuronal signals to and from the median preoptic nucleus (MnPO), which was shown to host the behavioral output neurons (Augustine et al., 2018), is beyond the scope of this study and is subject to future work.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current study and future research directions.

claim: It remains to be clarified if the increased c-fos signal in the SFO of GOF mice is directly caused by the tightened vessel phenotype, or indirectly affected by an altered angiocrine profile of the tightened endothelium, potentially leading to altered drinking behavior.
source: Moreover, it remains to be clarified if the increased c-fos signal in the SFO of GOF mice is directly caused by the tightened vessel phenotype, or indirectly affected by an altered angiocrine profile of the tightened endothelium, potentially leading to altered drinking behavior.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms underlying the observed neuronal activation.

claim: Preliminary analysis of primary mouse brain microvascular ECs (MBMECs) treated with Wnt3a revealed no regulation of VEGF that was previously described to be neuroactive.
source: Preliminary analysis of primary mouse brain microvascular ECs (MBMECs) treated with Wnt3a revealed no regulation of VEGF that was previously described to be neuroactive (data not shown) (Mackenzie and Ruhrberg, 2012).
evidence: This is a statement based on preliminary data not shown, and a citation to prior work.

claim: Preliminary experiments aiming to pharmacologically tighten CVO vessels with a systemically administered Wnt/β-catenin activator did not result in SFO vessel tightening.
source: Although own preliminary experiments aiming to pharmacologically tighten CVO vessels with a systemically administered Wnt/β-catenin activator did not result in SFO vessel tightening (data not shown), this might be a potential way to therapeutically modulate water intake.
evidence: This is a statement based on preliminary data not shown.

claim: Pharmacological modulation of SFO vessel permeability might be a potential way to therapeutically modulate water intake.
source: Although own preliminary experiments aiming to pharmacologically tighten CVO vessels with a systemically administered Wnt/β-catenin activator did not result in SFO vessel tightening (data not shown), this might be a potential way to therapeutically modulate water intake.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic applications.

claim: Patients that chronically receive LiCl, an FDA-approved drug for bipolar disorders and a potent Wnt/β-catenin activator, frequently develop polyuria that is linked to altered anti-diuretic hormone (ADH; vasopressin) function, which is released by the PP.
source: Interestingly, patients that chronically receive LiCl, an FDA-approved drug for bipolar disorders and a potent Wnt/β-catenin activator, frequently develop polyuria that is linked to altered anti-diuretic hormone (ADH; vasopressin) function, which is released by the PP.
evidence: This is a statement of established clinical knowledge.

claim: Many patients receiving LiCl develop polydipsia and urinate more frequently.
source: Moreover, many patients develop polydipsia and urinate more frequently (Malhi, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In-depth investigation of the pharmacologic modulation of SFO vessel permeability is required.
source: Hence in-depth investigation of the pharmacologic modulation of SFO vessel permeability is required.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: In light of the present work, the CVO vasculature likely participates actively in controlling water homeostasis.
source: Although the detailed mechanisms underlying the neuro-vascular coupling in the CVOs have to be investigated in more detail, in light of the present work however, the CVO vasculature likely participates actively in controlling water homeostasis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings of the study.
